title: Two Eids, not one
told: a saying of the Prophet ﷺ

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? what’s a celebration that comes back around every year that you really look forward to?
options: hold it in your mind. today is about two of them.
lovely. here are two more to know.
then let me show you two that come back every year.

steps.line: When the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ came to Medina, the people there kept two old yearly days of games and celebration.

steps.q: What do you think he told them about their two old feast days?
o: Keep both, but give thanks to God
Replace them with two better days
Keep one, and let the other go
steps.why: Anas reported it (Abu Dawud): God has given you better than those two, al-Adha and al-Fitr. Some scholars think the old days were Nayruz and Mihrajan, Persian seasonal feasts.

steps.line: “God has given you two better days,” he said: the day of sacrifice, and the day of breaking the fast. The two Eids.
Eid al-Fitr comes when Ramadan ends. Before its prayer, every family gives food for each person in it, so people in need can feast too.
steps.label: today

steps.q: This gift is called zakat al-fitr. A hadith calls it a purification for the one who fasted. Purification from what?
o: Any fasting days they had missed
Idle words and slips during the fast
The wealth they gained over the year
steps.why: Ibn ‘Abbas reported it as purification “from idle talk and foul words, and food for the poor.” Given before the Eid prayer it counts as zakat al-fitr; after, only as ordinary charity.

steps.line: Eid al-Adha, the day of sacrifice, remembers a story in the Qur’an. Ibrahim dreamed he must sacrifice his son, and asked the boy what he thought.
“Father, do as you are told,” his son said. “God willing, you’ll find me patient.” Then a voice called out, and a great sacrifice was given in the boy’s place.

steps.q: The Qur’an doesn’t name the son in this story. Who do most Muslims understand him to be?
steps.why: Most Muslim scholars say Ismail; some early ones said Ishaq. The Bible tells a related story with Isaac.

steps.line: On Eid al-Adha, families who are able offer an animal and share the meat with family, neighbors and people in need. On both Eids: “Eid Mubarak,” a blessed Eid.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Both Eids move through the seasons, a little earlier each year. Why?
o: Each country picks its own date
The Islamic calendar follows the moon
steps.why: A lunar year is about eleven days shorter than a solar one, so each Eid comes through every season in about 33 years. Many wait to sight the new crescent.

say: here’s what i love. both eids begin with a prayer and end at a crowded table, and both are built so nobody is left out.
in islam, the joy isn’t a break from faith. al-fitr gives thanks after a month of fasting. al-adha remembers ibrahim’s trust, and shares it out as food.

steps.q: The word Eid comes from a root meaning “to return.” Why is that a fitting name?
o: It’s a day that comes back around, every year
Pilgrims return home from Mecca on it
The food given is returned later
steps.why: A day that returns. Two feasts, coming back around every year.

today.say: think of one person who might not have a feast this season. share a meal, a plate or a small gift with them this week, the way eid makes room for everyone.
options: beautiful. that’s the whole spirit of both eids.
lovely. keep your eyes open. the extra chair is the point.

tomorrow.line: two words you’ve maybe heard a thousand times, and the peace folded inside them.

card.from: a saying of the Prophet ﷺ
sources: Sunan Abi Dawud 1134; Sunan an-Nasa’i 1556 (Anas: two old days of play in Medina; “God has given you something better: the day of al-Adha and the day of al-Fitr”)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1503 (zakat al-fitr, due for every person, given before people go out to the prayer)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1609 (zakat al-fitr as food for the poor; given before the prayer it is accepted zakat)
Qur’an 37:102–107 (Ibrahim’s dream; “O my father! Do that which thou art commanded. Allah willing, thou shalt find me of the steadfast”; the call; the ransom with “a tremendous victim”), paraphrased
Qur’an 22:28, 22:36 (eat of the sacrifice and feed the needy)
check: Caption 2 quotes Abu Dawud 1134 loosely (“God has given you something better than them”) as “two better days”. Confirm.

The Qur’an doesn’t name the son (most Muslims say Isma‘il); the lesson says “his son” and “the boy”. “A great sacrifice … in the boy’s place” follows 37:107; the painting shows a ram, the common understanding. Confirm.
The story of the dream is told gently and ends at the ransom, as flagged in the day-7 script; a Keeper should confirm it suits week one.
Painting EI1 shows old Medina’s festival with drums and cloths but no people. Confirm it fits the hadith (it only mentions “days of play”).
